title: There is no “Indian Question”
gist: Responding to a Chris Rufo/Jonathan Keeperman podcast titled 'The Indian Question', Noah Smith argues recent immigrants, including Indians, assimilate behaviorally as fast as past waves, that a 2020-2024 weakening of American identification among US-born Indian Americans is likely a defensive reaction to MAGA-era anti-Indian rhetoric, and that liberal-nationalist inclusion beats forced assimilation in building a shared American identity.

insights.claim: By behavioral measures such as English use, intermarriage, American names, income mobility and leaving enclaves, recent immigrant waves (Mexicans, Chinese, Indians) are assimilating as fast as or faster than European immigrants did a century or two ago.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Undercuts the empirical basis of restrictionist immigration policy narratives.
insights.quote: the recent waves of immigrants — Mexicans, Chinese people, Indians, and so on — are assimilating just as fast as or faster than the East and South European wave did a century ago

insights.claim: Pew surveys show later generations of Asian and Hispanic Americans are much more likely to identify simply as 'American', and less likely to call themselves 'global citizens', than immigrants themselves.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Generational identity convergence supports long-run social cohesion.
insights.locator: We do have lots of surveys about this

insights.claim: The Indian American Attitudes Survey showed second-generation Indian Americans far more likely than immigrants to identify as 'more American than Indian' in 2020, but by 2024 more US-born Indian Americans identified as 'more Indian than American' or 'equally' both.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: An early warning that political hostility may be reversing identity assimilation for a high-earning group.
insights.locator: In 2020, the Indian American Attitudes Survey

insights.claim: The lack of long-run longitudinal surveys on American versus ethnic identity means it is unclear whether identity shifts are generational effects or cohort effects driven by identity politics or the internet.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Data gaps leave room for competing political narratives on immigration.
insights.locator: Now, these could be generational effects

insights.claim: Smith hypothesizes that the 2024 rise in Indian ethnic identification among US-born Indian Americans was a reaction to the online Right's surge in anti-Indian attitudes that year, rather than to internet connectivity or identity politics, which were already present in 2020.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Hostile politics can erode integration of a key high-skill immigrant group.
insights.quote: my bet is that we’re seeing a reaction to the rise of the MAGA Right itself

insights.claim: Ethnic identity is defensive: people who feel excluded from the nation turn to their ethnic group for protection, so forced-assimilation campaigns suppress visible difference while strengthening ethnic identity.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Coercive assimilation policies are likely to increase social fragmentation, not cohesion.
insights.quote: forced-assimilation campaigns can suppress visible expressions of ethnic difference, but they strengthen ethnic identity itself
insights.locator: My argument is that this is exactly backwards

insights.claim: World War I forced-assimilation campaigns against German Americans led Germans overall to intermarry less and volunteer less in World War II.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that coercion backfires on national cohesion goals.
insights.quote: they caused Germans as a whole to intermarry less and to volunteer less in World War II
insights.locator: There’s plenty of evidence to support this

insights.claim: Anti-Hispanic rhetoric and perceived discrimination tend to increase Hispanic ethnic identification.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rhetoric-driven identity shifts can reshape voting coalitions.

insights.claim: Smith predicts the anti-Indian backlash sparked by Bo French's tweet and Rufo and Keeperman's 'Indian Question' podcast will push some Indian Americans to doubt America accepts them and to lean on co-ethnics for support.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising hostility could weaken the US draw for Indian talent central to the tech sector.
insights.locator: This pattern is likely to play out again

insights.claim: Smith argues mid-20th-century liberal nationalists such as FDR, Truman, Eisenhower and LBJ sought to create an 'American' ethnicity rather than a 'White' one, an effort that partially succeeded for Asians, Hispanics and Middle Easterners but not for Black Americans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Frames a policy template for national cohesion that neither current party pursues.

insights.claim: Smith contends neither the modern Right nor Left attempts broad American ethnogenesis: the Right fragments through suspicion and exclusion, while progressive POC/BIPOC categories were built in opposition to Whiteness and fell apart.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Persistent polarization and identity fragmentation remain a structural US political risk.
insights.quote: These are not nation-builders; they are nation-dismantlers.

insights.claim: Smith argues the shunning strategy toward right-wing figures in the 2010s failed, as anti-immigrant ideas took over the country despite remaining unpopular with the general public.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Minority-held policy positions can dominate politics, raising policy unpredictability.
insights.quote: Anti-immigrant ideas didn’t remain marginalized — in fact, they took over the country, despite their continued unpopularity among the general American public.

insights.claim: Smith frames the Abundance Agenda as an implicit expression of liberal nationalism, aiming to create abundance specifically for Americans.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a potential cross-ideological policy coalition around supply-side building.

insights.claim: Shared national identity underpins the ability to provide public goods and welfare states and likely increases tolerance of minorities.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Social cohesion is an input to fiscal capacity and policy stability.
insights.locator: I agree that this is extremely important
